entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Orvieto Cathedral (Duomo di Orvieto) in Umbria, central Italy, is one of the finest examples of Italian Gothic architecture, begun in 1290 CE to commemorate the Miracle of Bolsena (1263), and famous for Luca Signorelli's Last Judgment fresco cycle (1499-1504 CE) in the Chapel of San Brizio — a work that profoundly influenced Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling. The cathedral's polychrome marble façade, designed by Lorenzo Maitani, is considered the most beautiful Gothic facade in Italy.

The cathedral was built to house the Corporal of Bolsena — a linen cloth stained with blood from a eucharistic miracle in 1263, when a German priest's doubts about transubstantiation were resolved when the host bled. Pope Urban IV witnessed the relic, issued the bull Transiturus in 1264, and commissioned Thomas Aquinas to write Corpus Christi — the feast celebrating the Eucharist. Orvieto Cathedral was thus built to honor the theological controversy that produced one of Christianity's greatest feasts.

Luca Signorelli's frescoes in the San Brizio chapel (1499-1504) depicting the Antichrist, the End of Days, the Resurrection of the Dead, and the Damned Cast into Hell, are considered the most radical pre-Renaissance treatment of the Last Judgment. Michelangelo visited Orvieto specifically to study Signorelli's muscular, foreshortened figures before painting the Sistine Chapel — making Signorelli's work arguably the most influential fresco in Italian art history beyond Michelangelo himself.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Orvieto Cathedral's significance transcends architecture: its Signorelli frescoes directly influenced Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel, making it the overlooked link in Western art's greatest chain of inspiration.
